extracted.intended_audience: IP office staff, policymakers, IP statisticians, researchers, and trademark/patent professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methodological definitions for compiling, comparing and interpreting trademark (and related IP procedural) statistics across national and regional offices, including class counts, origin vs office data, timing metrics and data caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application class count (application class count)
rubrics_metrics.description: The total number of classes specified in applications – known as the application class count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class counts are used to make trademark registration internationally comparable. Because offices differ in filing systems (single-class vs multi-class), comparing class counts across offices improves international comparisons. This method for comparing offices began in 2004, the first year for which complete class count data are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Nice Classification and single vs multi-class filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Many offices use the Nice Classification, an international classification of goods and services for registering trademarks and service marks. Applications received at these offices are classified according to one or more of the 45 Nice classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some offices only allow single-class filing, requiring separate applications per class, while others permit multi-class filings. These differences affect raw application counts and motivate the use of application class counts for harmonized comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent application class count (regional multiplier)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application filed at a regional IP office is equivalent to filing an application in every member country of the organization that established that particular regional office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To calculate equivalent applications for the EUIPO, each application is multiplied by the number of EU member states (example: an EUIPO application filed by a non‑resident is counted as 27 applications abroad). The same multiplier is applied to the classes specified in such an application. The equivalent application class count concept is used for reporting data by origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office data vs Origin data (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark applications received by offices from resident and non-resident applicants are referred to as office data, whereas applications filed by applicants at a national or regional office (resident applications) or at foreign offices (applications abroad) are referred to as origin data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both perspectives are reported to complement the picture of trademark filing worldwide; users should be explicit which perspective they are using when comparing statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resident vs Non-resident filing (distinction and shares)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resident applications are those filed at a filer’s home or regional office; non-resident filings are those filed abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 2021 residents filing at home/regional offices accounted for 84% of global filing and non-resident filings 16%. Because filing behavior differs by jurisdiction, analyses should examine resident and non-resident shares separately and note trends (e.g., non-resident filing grew faster than resident filing in 2021).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of examiners (FTE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of examiners (FTE) where FTE is full time equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FTE counts are reported alongside procedural metrics; users should note that FTE definitions may vary and affect comparisons of office capacity and productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural timing metrics: First office action and Final office decision (months)
rubrics_metrics.description: First office action (months) and Final office decision (months) are reported procedural timing metrics for offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These timings are compiled across offices but are subject to procedural differences and measurement definitions. Because offices handle procedural steps differently, direct comparisons should be made cautiously and with awareness of local practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data comparability caveats (procedural differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every effort has been made to compile procedural data based on common definitions and concepts, but procedural differences make it extremely difficult to fully harmonize such data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'rejection' is not recorded as a final decision in Canada (applicants are informed of actions to take and if they cannot provide required information they are regarded as having abandoned the application). A similar situation exists in Australia. Analysts must account for such jurisdictional procedural differences when interpreting comparative indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not compare same-year applications to registrations directly
rubrics_metrics.description: After concluding the examination process, an office may decide to register a trademark. The number of registrations issued can fluctuate greatly from year to year, due in part to the varying amount of resources offices are able to dedicate to examining trademark applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For this reason, it is not possible to accurately compare the number of applications filed at a particular office in any given year with the number of registrations issued by that office in the same year. Users should avoid naive year-to-year application-to-registration comparisons without adjusting for processing lags and resource effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of origin reporting (equivalent grants by origin incomplete)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalent grants by origin data are incomplete, because some offices do not report by origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users relying on origin-based counts should check reporting completeness and account for missing origin breakdowns when aggregating or comparing origin statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping Nice classes into industry sectors for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: It is useful to group the 45 Nice classes into 10 industry sectors to offer insights into the relative importance of different goods and services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO groups Nice classes into sectors (e.g., research and technology, health, clothing and accessories, leisure and education, household equipment, agriculture, business services, chemicals, construction, transportation) and reports sectoral shares to show where applicants seek protection abroad. Analysts can adopt similar groupings for cross-office comparisons.
